_readme: Every user-facing string, heading, label, field table, navigation entry and empty
state the atlas renders lives in this file. assets/atlas.js contains no copy of its
own — it looks everything up here through assets/templates.js (window.AtlasUI).
To reword, reorder, retitle or re-theme the atlas, edit THIS file and re-run
which regenerates data/atlas.bundle.js. No JavaScript needs to change.
Three things you can do here without touching code:
strings  — any value may contain {{placeholders}}; the renderer fills them.
fields   — each views.*.fields array defines a key/value table row by row.
{ label, from } reads a property off the item; { label, compute }
calls a named computation registered in atlas.js (see COMPUTED);
delete a row to hide it, reorder rows to reorder the table.
theme    — cssVars are written onto :root at boot, overriding assets/atlas.css.
This file is curated, not generated. An atlas update rewrites data/atlas.json;
it must never rewrite this file.

_rail: `icon` names a glyph in assets/icons.js — never a Unicode character, because
these carry meaning. `requires` names an atlas.json collection; the entry is
hidden when that collection is absent or empty ('updated' is the special case
for 'more than one update has happened').
_search: kindLabels turns an atlas.json collection name into the reader's word for it.
A missing key falls back to the raw collection name, so adding a collection
degrades to something honest rather than to a blank.
_sectionTitles: Short names for the sections that have no title in atlas.json — the auth and
delivery singletons. Used anywhere an item is listed by name (the progress
checklist, search results, the What changed? list), where the view's own
sentence-length heading would be too long.

_tour: The one ordered route through every tracked section. Stages are defined by
atlas.json COLLECTION NAME, never by a list of ids — so a regenerated atlas
files each new section into the right stage automatically instead of leaving
a dead id behind. Order within a stage is that collection's authored order.
Reorder the walkthrough by reordering `stages`; drop a stage by deleting it.

tour.heading: The full tour
tour.lede: Every section in the atlas, in an order where each stop makes the next one easier: what the pieces are, how they talk to each other, what they store, what they do end to end, and finally how to change any of it. Stop and resume whenever — the atlas remembers where you were.
tour.doneBody: All {{total}} stops are marked complete. Reopen any of them from the completion checklist — nothing here locks.

stages.title: The islands
stages.blurb: What the pieces are, from the screen a visitor touches down to the stores that outlive every request.

stages.title: The routes between them
stages.blurb: How the islands actually talk — the mechanism behind each line on the map, and what happens when one of them fails.

stages.title: What travels
stages.blurb: The records the system keeps: what each one means in the real world, and where it is written down.

stages.title: Whole journeys
stages.blurb: End-to-end runs, step by step — from a person taking an action to the system producing a visible result.

stages.title: Who is allowed
stages.blurb: Identity, roles, and what each role may do — the rules every other section assumes.

stages.title: The depths
stages.blurb: The subsystems worth understanding on their own terms before you touch them.

stages.title: Getting it out
stages.blurb: How the project is tested, built, and delivered.

stages.title: Changing it yourself
stages.blurb: The exact files to open for the changes people most often need to make. This is what the rest of the tour was for.

Start the atlas with `node scripts/serve-atlas.mjs .` to keep it in `progress/progress.json` on disk instead — this browser's history is adopted automatically the first time you do.
